subcomponents.title: Uses scene-kit APIs without bypassing or duplicating them

criteria.rationale: The Talk boundary and the shared Scene boundary both consume the kit's public API without reimplementing it. Talk.tsx renders the kit's `Presentation` with `steps={STEPS}`, `title` and `initialMode`. It builds no nav, stage, chrome or fit-scale logic of its own. Scene.tsx imports `Appear, Arrow, Box, Frame, Label, SceneLayer, SymbolChip` and `SceneProps` from the kit barrel. It composes the whole diagram from them, passing ids to the kit nodes and wrapping the transient content in `Appear` inside `AnimatePresence`. Each step module is a `Step<SceneState>` object with `scene: Scene`, a `payload` and a `groupKey`, which is the kit's step contract. `Stage` then mounts `step.scene` with the payload. The demo adds no parallel layout, animation or navigation mechanism.

Scene.tsx imports Appear, Arrow, Box, Frame, Label, SceneLayer, SymbolChip, SceneProps from presentation-kit
Scene.tsx: `Scene({ payload }: SceneProps<SceneState>)` returns `<SceneLayer>` containing kit nodes
steps/index.ts: STEPS = [s1..s9]; 01-topic.tsx through 09-reveal.tsx each export `step: Step<SceneState>` with scene, payload and groupKey 'story'
Stage.tsx: `const Scene = step.scene; <Scene payload={step.payload} stepIndex={stepIndex} />`
judging basis: consensus-pass

subcomponents.title: Uses stable identities and appropriate grouped-scene architecture

criteria.rationale: Grouping: all nine step modules set `groupKey: 'story'` and `scene: Scene`. `Presentation` passes the active step to `Stage`, and `Stage` keys its single `motion.div` with `sceneKey(step)`. `sceneKey` returns `group:story` whenever `groupKey` is defined, so navigating between any two steps keeps the same key. The existing scene instance is therefore updated with a new `payload` instead of being remounted. The `LayoutGroup` and `AnimatePresence` in Stage enclose that mount. Identity: this is separate from groupKey. The presentation-owned `ENTITY_IDS` (imported in Scene.tsx as `E`) are passed as the `id` prop of `Box`, `Frame`, `Label`, `SymbolChip` and `Arrow`. `Box`, `Frame`, `Label` and `SymbolChip` forward `id` to `layoutId={id}` on a `layout` `motion.div` or `motion.span`, with `LAYOUT_TRANSITION`. The persisting `E.you` Box keeps the same layoutId across all nine beats. Box ids passed through `StepCard` (card1 to card3) and the `E.verify` Box are also layoutIds. Arrow uses `id` as `data-presentation-entity`, and its line endpoints animate through `motion.line` `animate`. Every ENTITY_IDS member is consumed by a rendered element in Scene.tsx, so none is dead.
evidence: 01-topic.tsx to 09-reveal.tsx: each has `scene: Scene`, `payload: { beat: N }` (N = 1..9) and `groupKey: 'story'`

Stage.tsx: `<motion.div key={sceneKey(step)} ...><Scene payload={step.payload} .../>`
Scene.tsx: `<Box id={E.you} ...>` plus E.* ids on Box, Frame, Label, SymbolChip and Arrow, and `StepCard id={E.card1..3}`

entities.ts: ENTITY_IDS members all referenced in Scene.tsx

subcomponents.title: Maintains clear boundaries and scope discipline

criteria.rationale: Code is split along clear lines. The registry (presentations/index.ts) lazy-loads Talk. Talk.tsx is a thin orchestration that wires STEPS, the title and the presentation CSS into the kit. entities.ts holds the id namespace. Each step module holds only narration and a beat payload. Scene.tsx holds the diagram, and talk.css holds the styling. The kit has no demo-specific logic. I traced the public contracts and found no dead ones. The required `title` prop of `Presentation` is consumed, not ignored: it becomes `data-presentation-name` on the chrome root. Every `ENTITY_IDS` member is used as an id in Scene.tsx. `SceneState` is imported by all nine steps. The optional `brand` and `symbol` inputs are rendered by Header and SymbolChip when supplied, so they are not misleading dead code. Duplicate ownership is minor: the title string is repeated in the registry and Talk.tsx, and Scene.tsx re-imports talk.css. Neither is a dead or misleading contract.

criteria.rationale: All four copies use the same cleanup. In both verify copies, `startPreview` spawns `process.execPath` on `viteBin()`, which is node_modules/vite's own bin file, with `detached: true`. So the preview server is the direct child, not an npm or npx wrapper. `stopChild` sends SIGTERM to the whole process group, escalates to SIGKILL after 3s, and awaits the child's 'exit'. In verify `main()`, the browser launch, render checks, the expected-step mismatch throw and every other error all happen after `preview = await startPreview()` inside one try. Judge C argues the SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP handlers call a synchronous `killAll()` without awaiting the exit. That path is outside the four exit paths the requirement and guidance name. Even there, `killAll` SIGKILLs the whole preview process group, so no wrapper-only kill leaves a server running. That reason does not decide the requirement.

criteria.rationale: No test hardcodes a port. Every test that starts a preview or browser does it through verify.mjs or inspect-presentation.mjs. The in-process inspect test calls `inspectPresentation({ root: copy })`, which calls `startPreview(root)` imported from './verify.mjs' (inspect-presentation.mjs:7, 195). `startPreview` takes `port ??= await freePort()`, and freePort listens on port 0, so the OS assigns a free port. It passes `--strictPort`. Cleanup is the same mechanism every time. The preview is the vite node process itself, spawned detached, and `stopChild` SIGTERMs or SIGKILLs its process group and awaits its exit. verify `main()` and `inspectPresentation` both call it in `finally`. The browser is closed in those same finally blocks. The e2e tests parse the allocated port and assert `portOpen(port)` is false after the passing run and after every fault run. runNode and bootstrap's run() spawn node or npm directly and await 'close'. Bootstrap's npm ci, build and lint are one-shot commands that exit, not servers. Its verify run spawns node directly on verify.mjs. Each test uses its own repo copy or temp dir, removed in afterAll. Judge C argues that a watchdog SIGKILL on timeout bypasses the script's cleanup and leaves the detached preview running. That only happens on a test timeout, which the guidance does not name. In every delivered test run the processes are terminated through the scripts' finally cleanup, so that reason does not decide the requirement.

criteria.rationale: I agree with Judge C's fail. Most of the agent-driven skill journeys in requirement-002 are excluded for an environmental reason: the runner has no agent invocation surface. Those journeys therefore do not count against coverage. Two groups of allowed behaviors still remain unexercised. 1. **Render verification and pass/fail reporting (requirement-003).** The log says `npm run verify` was never run (line 1078). It also says verifier failure injection was not run (lines 1058 and 1088). That leaves these scenarios unexercised: "Missing sample fails", "Console or page error fails verification", "Step error fails verification" and "Clear outcome". Nothing in the environment prevented these runs. The stated reason is that the acceptance skill rules them out of scope, which is a workflow choice. Under the criterion, an omission disclosed for a non-environmental reason still counts in proportion to what it leaves unexercised. 2. **Motion sequencing (requirement-001).** The scene-continuity observation at line 1063 checks only DOM identity ("the data-presentation-scene element stayed the same"), that `you` stayed in place, and that entities were present or absent after settling. The criterion names this case directly: DOM persistence instead of motion sequencing does not cover the scenario. So "Persisting entity morphs", "New entity enters after others settle" and "Continuing entities are not faded as newcomers" are not covered. Line 1089 also disclaims mid-transition scoring. 3. **Unstyled kit output and typed payloads.** Line 1098 says these were not exercised. Mounting an unstyled consumer does not need an agent, so blaming the unavailable agent surface does not make this gap environmental. Taken together, these candidate-chosen omissions leave a substantial share of the allowed behavior unexercised. That share covers the core of requirement-003's verifier and the motion half of the stable-entities and grouped-scene requirements. Judges A and B pass the criterion on the grounds that every omission was disclosed or environmental. The cited lines do not support that. Workflow-prohibited verifier runs are disclosed but not environmental, so under the criterion they count in proportion. Neither judge addresses the fact that the transition observation checks only DOM persistence, which the criterion explicitly says does not cover motion sequencing.

The catch block prints `FAIL verify [sample]` and returns 1, and process.exit uses that code (lines 306-312 and 319-321). So a missing sample is reported by an explicit check that names the sample phase, which is what the guidance credits. The E2E test also renames the registered slug and asserts a non-zero exit plus `FAIL verify [sample]` (tests/e2e/verify.test.ts:57, 72-79). Judge B's reason does not decide this criterion. B's case is a reorder of the STEPS array in steps/index.ts with the literals left untouched. That is a hypothetical edit the candidate never produces, and the guidance does not name it. The fixture requirement is that verification fails when the sample is absent. B agrees that missing registrations and missing literals are rejected, and the source also checks literal order across the step files. The guidance does not require a dedicated test once the check is explicit.

votes.rationale: The props are typed from the element's props (HTMLMotionProps<'div'>, SVGProps and HTMLAttributes), and kit-only props such as Icon, symbol, order, active and the Arrow geometry are destructured, not forwarded. The identity-hooks clause fails, though. Every primitive sets its data-presentation-* hooks before `{...rest}`, so a caller can override them. Box, Frame, Label, SymbolChip and Emphasis set `data-presentation-entity` and `data-presentation-node` first. Arrow sets `data-presentation-entity` and `data-presentation-node` before `{...rest}`. Appear sets `data-presentation-appear` first, and SceneLayer sets `data-presentation-scene-layer` first. Arrow's `style` is also merged after its defaults.

votes.rationale: Props are properly typed (`HTMLMotionProps<'div'>`, `SVGProps`, `HTMLAttributes`) and kit-only props such as Icon, order, symbol, from/to, width/height and active are stripped before the DOM. The identity-hook clause fails. In `Box`, `Frame`, `Label`, `SymbolChip`, `Emphasis`, `Appear`, `Arrow` and `SceneLayer`, `{...rest}` is spread after `layoutId`, `data-presentation-entity`, `data-presentation-node` and other data-presentation-* attributes. The step-identification part is not met for the first step. In renderPresentation, `current` starts at 0, and the console and pageerror listeners record `step: current` (verify.mjs:224-227). first_results.rationale: In verify.mjs, startPreview spawns the Vite bin directly with process.execPath and detached:true. The child is therefore the preview server itself, not an npm or npx wrapper. stopChild sends SIGTERM to the process group (-child.pid), escalates to SIGKILL after 3s, and awaits the child's 'exit' event. verify main() calls startPreview, launchBrowser and every check inside one try. Its finally awaits preview.stop(), so success, a failing check, a launchBrowser PhaseError, and any later throw all stop and await the server. A readiness failure inside startPreview awaits stopChild before throwing. inspectPresentation calls launchBrowser and every capture inside a try whose finally awaits preview.stop(). The bootstrap copies have the same code at the same lines (detached:true at 170, group kill at 197-198, finally stop at 315, inspect stop at 229), and bootstrap.test.ts asserts they are identical. I rule A's and B's pass. Judge C's reason is that the SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP handlers call the synchronous killAll() and do not await. That reason does not decide the criterion. The exit paths the guidance names are success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and an error after the preview started, and all of them go through the awaited finally. External signals are not one of those paths. Even there, killAll SIGKILLs the whole process group, so the server is still terminated.

So the preview server is the direct child, not an npm or npx wrapper. `stopChild` sends SIGTERM to the whole process group, escalates to SIGKILL after 3s, and awaits the child's 'exit'. first_results.rationale: I agree with Judge C's fail. Most of the agent-driven skill journeys in requirement-002 are excluded for an environmental reason: the runner has no agent invocation surface. Those journeys therefore do not count against coverage. Two groups of allowed behaviors still remain unexercised. 1. **Render verification and pass/fail reporting (requirement-003).** The log says `npm run verify` was never run (line 1078). It also says verifier failure injection was not run (lines 1058 and 1088). That leaves these scenarios unexercised: "Missing sample fails", "Console or page error fails verification", "Step error fails verification" and "Clear outcome". Nothing in the environment prevented these runs. The stated reason is that the acceptance skill rules them out of scope, which is a workflow choice. Under the criterion, an omission disclosed for a non-environmental reason still counts in proportion to what it leaves unexercised. 2. **Motion sequencing (requirement-001).** The scene-continuity observation at line 1063 checks only DOM identity ("the data-presentation-scene element stayed the same"), that `you` stayed in place, and that entities were present or absent after settling. The criterion names this case directly: DOM persistence instead of motion sequencing does not cover the scenario. So "Persisting entity morphs", "New entity enters after others settle" and "Continuing entities are not faded as newcomers" are not covered. Line 1089 also disclaims mid-transition scoring. 3. **Unstyled kit output and typed payloads.** Line 1098 says these were not exercised. Mounting an unstyled consumer does not need an agent, so blaming the unavailable agent surface does not make this gap environmental. Taken together, these candidate-chosen omissions leave a substantial share of the allowed behavior unexercised. That share covers the core of requirement-003's verifier and the motion half of the stable-entities and grouped-scene requirements. Judges A and B pass the criterion on the grounds that every omission was disclosed or environmental. The cited lines do not support that. Workflow-prohibited verifier runs are disclosed but not environmental, so under the criterion they count in proportion. Neither judge addresses the fact that the transition observation checks only DOM persistence, which the criterion explicitly says does not cover motion sequencing.

verification-tooling.rationale: The review guidance for verification-step-error-fails says to fail when the check converts an absent or non-numeric hook into a number that still satisfies its comparison, and gives Number(null) === 0 on the first step as its example. scripts/verify.mjs reads the index as Number(await chrome.getAttribute('data-step-index')) and checks only `!== 0`. A missing attribute becomes Number(null) === 0 and passes the start check as if it were valid progress. Later steps are checked by exact string equality, but a one-step presentation never reaches that check, so a missing hook goes unnoticed. The sound step-count check and the stalled-transition test do not save the pass, because the guidance treats this conversion as an independent reason to fail.

engineering-quality.rationale: The contradiction does not hold. The requirement says every wait for preview readiness must have a timeout, and both startPreview() copies do: the polling loop is bounded by `const deadline = Date.now() + 30000`. It also stops early if the child exits, then stops the child and throws a PhaseError('preview', ...). The auditor's argument depends on one fetch() hanging forever against a server that accepts the connection but never answers. Neither the material nor the review guidance establishes that scenario, and the rule is not to fail a criterion on a hypothetical the guidance does not name. Before vite preview listens, fetch is refused at once and the loop retries. After it listens, it answers. Node's built-in fetch also has its own default connect and header timeouts, so even the hypothetical hang would end. The plain meaning of 'has a timeout' is met by the 30-second deadline; the guidance does not ask for a timeout on each request. The auditor also accepts that the other two clauses hold: runBuild() uses spawnSync and finishes before startPreview(), and readiness is checked over HTTP rather than by parsing printed output, so the parsing clause does not apply. The other waits in the inspect and verify copies are bounded too (chrome.waitFor timeout 10000; waitForFunction timeouts 5000 and 3000).
evidence: Both verify.mjs copies, startPreview(): `const deadline = Date.now() + 30000; while (Date.now() < deadline) { if (exited) break; try { const res = await fetch(`${url}/`) ... } catch {} ... } await…
Both verify.mjs copies, runBuild(): uses `spawnSync('npm', ['run', 'build'], ...)`. In main(), `runBuild()` runs before `startPreview()`. In inspectPresentation(), `runBuild(r…
Readiness polls over HTTP with fetch, and stdout/stderr are only collected into a log for error messages. No printed ready URL is parsed, so the ANSI/chunk clause does not apply.
Other readiness waits are bounded: `chrome.waitFor({ state: 'attached', timeout: 10000 })` and `waitForFunction(..., { timeout: 5000 })` in inspect; `{ timeout: 3000 }` in verify.
The auditor's defect needs a server that accepts the connection but never responds. Nothing in the material shows that behaviour, and the review guidance does not name it.
